comment:
Access to clean air is crucial for one to enjoy life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Thus, all regulation enforcing the Clean Air Act is crucial to keeping American air clean. This proposed rule, involving revisions to the Federal Air Rules for Reservations (FARR), focuses on particulate matter emissions as well as visible emissions on Reservation lands. While some of these revisions are beneficial to keeping air clean, there are issues that should be reviewed.
It is important to keep track of emissions being put into the air by stationary sources, as they are often the most impactful on the environment. This proposed rule however gives “the approval of shorter sampling times or smaller sample volumes when necessitated by process variables or other factors” (Section II, Subsection A, Paragraph 13). Creating too much flexibility for attaining sample numbers is dangerous without specifying clearly what “process variables or other factors” can require such. Thus, these such things should be clearly spelled out in this proposed rule, or examples of such scenarios should be provided.
Regarding orchard heating devices, it is beneficial that they are no longer exempt from the visible emissions limit, as the diesel fuel emissions can be harmful, as explained in this proposed rule. This would then set the limit to be consistent with that of FARR, however it also states that this would not go into effect until three years after, with two year extensions also being available, if one can show that no alternative is accessible. These time frames are quite lenient for emissions that can put large amounts of carbon dioxide into the air, and thus they should be shortened to two years and one year if extended.
Pollution sources within the United States must be monitored to ensure the air Americans are breathing is up to the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). If allowed to have shorter sampling and smaller sample volumes, this can skew accurate representations of emissions from any source. Accurate monitoring or modeling requires accurate measurements, thus, the flexibility of this proposed rule could have negative effects on such monitoring. To correct this, examples of specific situations should be provided in this regulation, so it is not as ambiguous. This would prevent all situations from having a case of being able to be approved for shorter sample periods or smaller sample volumes, when it is not seriously necessitated.
As stated previously, in this proposed rule, orchard heating devices are subject to visible emissions limits consistent with that of FARR. The devices may not produce visible emissions with opacity exceeding 20%, averaged over a six minute period. However, the proposed rule states that it will not go into effect until three years after this rule is passed. This is too long of a time frame regarding harmful, strong concentration emissions of carbon dioxide. Even if new technology is not available to those using these devices, they require frequent cleaning that should keep their visible emissions to a minimum and within the bounds of this regulation. From a study done by Robert Kepner, of the Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources in California, looking at the reduction of smoke produced by these devices, he concludes that “the introduction of air through the smaller regulating holes, the reduction of air leakage around the edges of the regulator, and the uniform burning rates obtainable with this device are all factors which tend to reduce the soot accumulations and the corresponding smokiness”. He then goes on to state “these heaters should not be operated for more than 10 to 12 hours without cleaning” (Kepner 14). These orchard heating devices can produce large amounts of visible emissions, however with proper operation and care, they can be kept well within the bounds of the limit. Thus, these timelines mentioned in the proposed rule can be shortened significantly, as the operators can directly affect the amounts of emissions produced.
Protecting clean air is of utmost importance when it comes to environmental regulation. This proposed rule looks to ensure visible and particulate matter emissions are kept consistent with FARR limits, positively affecting air quality. However, in order to ensure this air quality, examples where smaller sample volumes or shorter sample periods can be allowed must be provided, as well as faster enactment of limits on emissions from orchard heating devices are useful revisions to this proposed rule. This is to make certain that all pollution is accounted for in monitoring or sampling, as well as simply keeping it out of the air.

comment:
While these regulations will likely improve air quality in the areas of concern in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington, the explanation section for certain new requirements concedes that some residential orchard heating devices will fail to comply with new standards. This means some people will need to replace their home heating methods in the next three years or apply for 2-year duration extensions. However, to qualify for an extension, residents have to prove there is no “reasonably available” alternative. This places a burden on residents in the reservations of the area and may cause financial problems for families trying to replace their wood-burning appliances. While the EPA says it will work with tribal programs to help alleviate potential funding problems, there is no clear guideline for how much aid residents would actually receive from the government for meeting the new air quality standards.
I think a better course of action would be to offer incentives for residences that choose to replace their heating appliances for EPA-approved appliances, instead of forcing all members to comply with the new regulation within the next three years. For example, a tax break awarded to residents who could prove they replaced their orchard heating appliance within the three-year timeframe could be an effective way to decrease air pollution while not burdening people who may not be able to afford a replacement option.
The reservation areas concerned in these regulations are in the northwest portion of the state, where winters can be harsh. Placing any strict limits on the modes of heating allowed in private residences means burdening the people of these areas financially, despite the marginal decrease in particulate matter air pollution that may follow the new rules. While I support reasonable methods to control particulate matter and other forms of air pollution, I do not think certain portions of this new regulation are fair or feasible.

comment:
This proposed rule seems to have many pros and cons. As I am not a resident of Idaho, Oregon, or Washington and I am not a part of any tribe in these areas I feel as if my opinion holds little value. Although I still feel as if my outside viewpoint may provide other helpful concerns, and it certainly may not but that’s not for me to decide. Since the Federal Air Rules for Regulations has not been updated since 2005 and it is now 2022 it is only logical to make revisions that maybe should have been put in place prior to this moment. Air pollution is a problem worldwide but all pollution, especially unregulated pollution, needs to be minimized as much as possible. I do agree that the reservations need to comply with the air standards that the rest of their states and country are following. With the information provided in this proposed rule about how different sized particles in the air affect the human body in negative aspects, it makes sense to want them to be as small as possible. I am not sure how much less than or equal to 2.5 micrometers in aerodynamic diameter and 35 micrograms per cubic meter in a 24-hour period actually is, but I think society should want the least amount of pollution and smallest particles to prevent harm to the body as well as the land.
From reading other comments on this proposed rule, it has come to my attention that one of the most controversial aspects is the need for the reservations and the people on them will only be able to use wood burning devices that are approved by the Environmental Protection Agency. It seems as if this rule is targeting wood burning devices as a large source of unregulated pollution so this makes me believe they are almost a necessity for the people on the reservation and are used daily or a lot of the time. If EPA approved wood burning devices are going to be mandatory, they need to be affordable for the citizens on the reservations to replace if they are using devices not approved by the EPA. Also, it seems like there needs to be some motivation for people to switch to EPA approved devices rather than just air quality. I am sure some of these devices can be pretty expensive so maybe there could be some sort of trade in program. Overall, this rule seems to have positive intent for the citizen’s and the land’s wellbeing, but there may need to be some tweaks in order to get the citizens on board with the switch in wood burning devices.

comment:
I found this regulation interesting because of the long duration of time between air quality policy changes in Indian reservations. Granted, it is important to recognize their sovereignty and ability to make their own decisions regarding air pollution and overall quality. However, it is likely that many Indian reservation members were unaware of their poor quality, what they were doing to worsen it, and what they might do to improve it. With that being said, I was interested to see how the EPA addressed this issue given that it had not been re-visited in nearly two decades.
When reading this regulation initially, many readers were likely concerned about the EPA overstepping their boundaries and making policy changes in a sovereign area. However, those feelings are unnecessary, as section D specifically states that numerous discussions were had between the EPA and Tribe members to ensure that the new policies were agreed upon. Moreover, some may also have concern that the primary target of this new policy (wood burning, outdoor fires, etc.) would inflict on some of the traditional practices among the tribes. However, sections were included granting exceptions for outdoor fires and cultural practices with “traditional purposes” in the general rules section of the regulation. Given that the primary concerns were met with reasonable policy, there are no major holes that seem to require filling before this regulation passes. This leaves my only complaint being the complete lack of attention being paid to air quality in Indian reservations since 2005
I believe that all environmental policymakers can agree that the most significant steps toward cleaner air have taken place in the years following 2005, primarily during the Obama administration from 2008-2016. In the 17 years since the 2005 FARR, how is it possible that no one thought to monitor air quality in Indian reservations and implement policy to improve it? While they are sovereign states, it is well known that they likely lack the technology and expertise to monitor their own air quality and make changes where they see fit. In summary; yes now is better than never, but 17 years is far too long to ignore necessary change.
This regulation seems like a set of well-planned policy changes that address the poor air quality in and around Indian reservations. As a reader, I was glad to read that the opinions of those living in the reservations were supposedly taken into consideration and implemented into the plan. In the future, it is important to remember that Indian reservations must be apart of our nation’s journey toward cleaner air and environment, and I hope that future policy reflects that.

comment:
I heat my shop and house with wood in our rural area north of Orofino, ID. I support smoke management regulations, but want to make sure that they don't become impractical for country living.
1. Residential Woodstove Installation: a. I oppose the requirement that a woodstove must be EPA approved. As a structural firefighter, I have seen numerous chimney fires that resulted from improper use of woodstoves. All of these stove were EPA approved. The EPA approval is a false insurance, because people think they can run them dampered down all day long, which in turn builds up an excessive amount of particulates in the emissions, resulting in creosote buildup in the chimney and particulates in the air. I recommend wording that requires woodstoves to be operated in a manor to reduce excessive smoke/particulates and not require EPA stove certification.
b. Does the definition of "residential woods stove" also apply to a heater in a shop? If so, I strongly disagree with a shop heater being EPA approved, but I do believe they should be operated to reduce emissions.
c. The rule changes specifies that stoves can only burn fuels designed for these devices. What about paper, which I use to start my fires? I recommend broadening the definition of burnable fuels to include paper products.
2. Residential Woodstove Curtailment: a. I agree wit hthe rule to control burning when smoke exceeds certain levels. However, I would like to see the curtailment areas broken down into landscape areas that reflect different air dispersion. I live in the hills 7 miles north of Orofino. Most of the time when Orofino is socked in by smoke in the winter when there is poor air dispersion in the valley, we have good air dispersion up in the hills. The valleys and the hills should be defined in a way to allow them to be treated differently.

comment: This proposed rule illustrates positive intentions from the government to protect both the human health and the environment of communities on reservations. However, based on other comments made by people who will be directly impacted by this rule, it seems this rule needs to better account for the needs of residents. Although improvements in air quality will certainly benefit residents of these reservations, the accessibility of these improvements must be considered. Prohibiting all wood burning devices that are not approved by the Environmental Protection Agency will likely burden these residents in their day to day life, which may not be a sacrifice these communities are willing to make for the sake of cleaner air. Environmental Justice needs to be considered more seriously in this proposed rule, as it is likely that much of the air pollution these communities face is not self-inflicted and should not be framed as such. Information clarity should be prioritized moving forward so that affected communities can prepare for these changes, and plan for accommodations. There should also be a system or program in place to transition these communities to more sustainable heat sources at low costs if this rule moves forward.
